summary.one_line: A Haryana solar-pump EPC contractor that earns ~97% of revenue from state agencies under PM-KUSUM, now raising ~₹61 cr fresh (plus a ₹7.35 cr promoter OFS) mostly to fund receivables and a module-line expansion. Reported profits have jumped, but it has no real moat, operating cash flow has not followed profit, its main subsidy scheme's Phase I expired in March 2026, and the governance record has too many lapses.
bull_points: Profitability stepped up sharply: PAT rose from ₹4.95 cr (FY24) to ₹16.43 cr (FY25) and ₹20.67 cr (FY26) on revenue of ₹138.3 cr → ₹142.4 cr → ₹170.3 cr, as low-priced legacy EESL contracts were replaced by higher-rate SECI/state PM-KUSUM orders (S1).

Proven tender execution: won 11 of 14 valid tenders over three years, ranked among the five largest winners (1,748 pumps) in HAREDA's 24,484-pump PM-KUSUM award, and broke into Maharashtra, which was 45.5% of FY26 revenue (S1, S15, S14).
New 60 MW Mono-PERC module line at Karnal became operational on 20 March 2026 and is ALMM-listed and BIS-certified, which could let the company capture more of the value in each pump system (S1).
Leverage has fallen as profits were retained: debt/equity went from 2.28x (FY24) to 0.77x (FY26), and promoters keep 70.13% after the issue (S1, S3).
bear_points: Cash does not match profit: operating cash flow over FY24–FY26 adds up to about –₹3.7 cr against ~₹42 cr of cumulative PAT. Receivables rose to ₹125.3 cr (269 days), and ~₹60 cr was invoiced in the last three months of FY26 (S1).
Extreme concentration: top customer (HAREDA) was 50.0%/85.2%/88.5% of revenue in FY26/FY25/FY24, the top 10 customers were 100%, and government was 97.2% (S1).
The underlying demand driver is a subsidy scheme whose current phase ran 'till 31.03.2026'. PM-KUSUM 2.0 was still only 'likely to be announced' as of September 2026 (S9, S12).

Governance lapses: a Section 42 private-placement contravention is pending adjudication, a GST order (₹21.3 lakh) is based on ITC claimed on 'fake invoices', RoC filings were delayed, and figures in bank stock statements did not match the books (S1).
watch_points: Whether PM-KUSUM Phase II / 2.0 is notified and when Haryana and Maharashtra issue fresh Component-B tenders (S12, S17).
Collection of the ₹125 cr receivable book in FY27 against management's target of ~100 debtor days (S1).
Execution of the two ₹47.5 cr private 25 MW module orders (AVI Renewable, Ethos Power), placed in July 2025 and still fully unexecuted at 31 July 2026 (S1).
The outcome of the Section 42 adjudication, the GST fake-invoice ITC order and the HVR Solar criminal complaint (S1).

reasoning: The money mostly funds receivables, not new capability. ₹29.50 cr of the ₹44.60 cr of named uses is working capital, needed because debtor days went from 107 to 269 and FY24–FY26 operating cash flow was negative overall even as PAT reached ₹20.67 cr. Another ₹7.35 cr is an OFS that goes to the largest promoter, not the company (S1, S3).

Revenue is a single subsidy scheme channelled through two or three state agencies. Government was 97.2% of FY26 revenue, HAREDA alone 50–88% across three years, and PM-KUSUM's current phase ran only until 31 March 2026, with Phase II not yet notified as of September 2026 (S1, S9, S12).

There is no moat. The company won 1,748 of 24,484 pumps (~7%) in Haryana's 2024 award, against Oswal (6,471) and Shakti (4,573). Its pumps and controllers are made by an OEM, and its old module plant became obsolete in 2024 when MNRE efficiency rules changed (S1, S15).

The order book is thinner on the core business than the headline suggests. Of ₹140.2 cr unexecuted, about ₹95 cr is two private 25 MW module orders from July 2025 that had seen no execution a year later; the government pump backlog is only about ₹28 cr (S1).

Governance quality is below par, even for an SME: Section 42 contravention (share money used before allotment), a GST demand over ITC on fake invoices, repeated late RoC filings, mismatches between bank stock statements and the books, and FY26 accounts re-audited by a different peer-review auditor (S1).

Revisit only if Phase II is notified, receivables actually convert to cash, and the 160 MW line reaches commercial operation as scheduled (April 2027). None of these can be checked before this issue closes on 29 September 2026 (S1, S4).

subsections.title: What the company actually does and how it earns revenue

blocks.text: Himalayan Solar was incorporated in Panchkula, Haryana in September 2015 and became a public company in November 2024 (S1, S2). The RHP describes three verticals: EPC contracts (design, manufacture, supply, installation and commissioning of solar water pumping systems and small rooftop/inverter systems), support services under a skill-development training programme, and sale of solar products such as modules and cells (S1). In practice it is almost entirely one business: turnkey solar water pumps installed on farmers' land under state-run PM-KUSUM Component-B programmes, which made up 97.54% of FY26 revenue (S1).

blocks.caption: Segment-wise revenue from operations (₹ crore; restated, from RHP)

blocks.text: The pricing model is tender-based. State nodal agencies (HAREDA in Haryana, MSEDCL and MEDA in Maharashtra, PEDA in Punjab) empanel vendors at tender-discovered rates, and farmers choose among the empanelled suppliers ('market mode') (S16). In Haryana the farmer pays 25% and the rest is subsidy: 30% from the Centre and 45% from the state (S16). Final payment depends on the pump running for 90 days with water-discharge data uploaded to remote monitoring portals. The company says that in practice this often takes more than 180 days, which explains its long receivable cycle (S1).
The customer is effectively the state, not the farmer. Revenue depends on subsidy budgets, tender timing and government payment processes, not on end-demand the company can build itself (S1, S16).

In each pump system, the pump and the pump controller are made by an outside OEM and sold under the 'Himalayan Solar' brand. All other components apart from those two are bought from external vendors (S1). The company's own manufacturing is limited to solar PV modules. Its 2017 Panchkula plant (40 MW polycrystalline) ran at only 18.54% utilisation in FY23 and 22.98% in FY24, then stopped in August 2024 because MNRE's revised efficiency norms moved government demand to mono-PERC modules and made the line obsolete (S1).

blocks.caption: Manufacturing footprint (from RHP)
rows: Machinery not yet ordered; COD targeted Apr 2027

blocks.text: Suppliers are concentrated too. The top supplier was 29.0% of FY26 purchases (36.9% in FY25, 56.0% in FY24), and the top 10 were 98.0%. There are no long-term supply contracts (S1). Purchases are fully domestic, with 66.5% from Haryana-based vendors in FY26 (S1). The company runs a registered office, a Gurugram branch and 16 warehouses, mostly in Haryana district towns near installation sites, plus one each in Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh (S1). It had 87 employees as of 31 July 2026 (S3) and 40 dealers at 31 March 2026 (S1).

items: Delivery chain: win the tender or empanelment → farmer applies via the state portal (Saral in Haryana) → buy modules, OEM pumps/controllers and structures → install via a district warehouse network → 90-day performance and RMS data → payment claim (S1, S16).
Bank guarantees issued on the company's behalf (performance/tender security) grew to ₹29.18 cr at FY26 from ₹9.18 cr at FY24, a measure of how much execution risk is outstanding (S1).

blocks.caption: Customer and geographic concentration (% of revenue from operations)

blocks.text: FY26 diversification was real but narrow: revenue moved from one state agency to two, with Maharashtra's MSEDCL/MEDA pump programmes rising to 45.5% (S1). The company had only 11 customers in all of FY25 (S1).

blocks.caption: Unexecuted order book at 31 July 2026 (₹ crore)

blocks.text: The RHP says the order book 'majorly consists of contracts from Government departments', but its own table shows ~₹109 cr of the ₹140 cr (about 78%) is private. The two 25 MW module orders (₹95 cr) were placed in July 2025 and had not been executed at all a year later (S1). The government pump backlog, which is the core business, is only about ₹31 cr including the NSDC order.

subsections.title: Market size and the PM-KUSUM dependency

blocks.text: Demand comes from PM-KUSUM Component B, which targets 14 lakh stand-alone solar agriculture pumps. MNRE's scheme page lists its duration as 'till 31.03.2026' (S9). A June 2026 guide likewise describes the scheme as extended through March 2026 with 'a Phase II expected to follow' (S17). As of 14 September 2026 the Union minister had said PM-KUSUM 2.0, with a new agrivoltaics component, is 'likely to be announced' soon. No notified guidelines or targets had been reported (S12).

Market-size estimates depend heavily on scope. IMARC puts India's solar water pump equipment market at USD 120.8 million in 2025, growing at a 6.91% CAGR to USD 236.9 million by 2034 (S13). Sector commentary cites a much larger theoretical opportunity (₹5.5 trillion including diesel-pump replacement) and a ₹34,422 cr PM-KUSUM allocation (S10). For this company, the relevant 'market' is simply the annual volume of state Component-B tenders, which is set by government budgets.

The key industry risk is a gap between scheme phases. With Phase I formally ended and Phase II not yet notified, new state tenders may slow in FY27 just as the company is betting on growth (S9, S12, S17).

Listed leaders dominate the segment. Oswal Pumps is described as holding around 38% of PM-KUSUM solar pump volumes and Shakti Pumps around 25% (S11). Shakti reported FY26 revenue of ₹2,697.6 cr and has installed 1,52,594 pumps under the scheme. Oswal reported FY26 revenue of ₹2,064.4 cr and is backward-integrating into 2.1 GW of modules. Australian Premium Solar's pump division alone did ₹308 cr in FY26 (S10). IMARC also lists C.R.I. Pumps, KSB and Lubi among the key players (S13). Unlike Himalayan Solar, the top two make their own pumps and motors.

The table (S15, S14) shows that even in its home state and main customer, Himalayan Solar is a mid-sized empanelled vendor with about 7% of the award, not a dominant supplier. Shares are computed from the reported pump counts.

No real moat is visible. Empanelment is open to many vendors, and in Haryana the farmer picks among them (S16). The pump and controller, the parts that differentiate a system, are outsourced to an OEM (S1). Module manufacturing is commoditised, and the company's own 40 MW line became obsolete overnight when MNRE changed efficiency norms (S1). Its 'competitive strengths' in the RHP are generic: magazine rankings, 'strong relationships', certifications (S1).

items: What counts in its favour: a high tender win rate (11 of 14 valid bids over three years), ALMM listing and BIS certification of the new mono-PERC modules, and a track record with HAREDA since FY21-22 (S1).

What doesn't count: there is no import-substitution position, no market-share claim, and no proprietary technology. The capex buys standard Chinese line equipment from ChinTiyan New Energy (Hubei), which any competitor can also buy (S1).

blocks.text: The competitive position is that of a price-taking empanelled contractor. The margin jump from FY24 to FY25 came from tender rates being reset higher (SECI vs legacy EESL rates), which the company does not control (S1).

blocks.caption: Restated P&L (₹ crore; FY ending March). EBITDA computed as PBT + finance cost + D&A − other income

blocks.text: All figures are computed from the restated statements in the RHP (S1). Aggregator summaries match on revenue, PAT, net worth and borrowings, but quote a slightly different EBITDA (₹29.04 cr for FY26), probably because of a different treatment of other income (S3).

The story is a margin reset, not steady growth. Revenue went from about ₹47 cr in FY23 to ₹138 cr in FY24, then grew only 3% in FY25 and 19.6% in FY26 (S1). The big profit change came in FY25, when gross margin jumped from 8% to 21% with flat revenue. Management attributes this to legacy fixed-price EESL contracts (June 2021–August 2023, with no escalation clause) giving way to SECI and state PM-KUSUM orders 'awarded at substantially higher rates' (S1). FY26 other income includes a ₹1.05 cr insurance claim (S1).

Margins depend on government tender prices. The FY23 PAT margin of ~1.24% under fixed-rate EESL contracts shows how quickly this business's profitability can collapse when tender rates lag input costs (S1).

Leverage looks fine on the headline ratio but thin on coverage: the RHP's own debt-service coverage ratio was 0.80 in FY26 and 0.70 in FY25 (S1). Total assets grew by ₹64 cr in FY26, and almost all of it is receivables (+₹59 cr), funded partly by stretching suppliers to 181 days (S1). Of the ₹66.07 cr of payables, ₹63.46 cr is owed to just five material creditors, and ₹20.37 cr is owed to MSMEs (S1). MSME payables are subject to a statutory 45-day payment rule, which makes 181-day creditor days hard to sustain.

Red flag: the RHP says ~₹60 cr of invoices were raised in the last three months of FY26, and that some projects 'had not reached the requisite execution milestones' needed to submit payment claims. About ₹17 cr of receivables are retention money (S1). Revenue booked in Q4 but not yet claimable deserves scepticism.

subsections.title: Cash flow vs profit: does the trend support the story?

blocks.caption: Profit vs operating cash flow (₹ crore)
rows: Operating cash flow before WC changes

blocks.text: Over three years the business has reported ₹42 cr of profit and produced negative operating cash (S1). All growth has been funded by bank lines, supplier credit and, now, IPO money. The company's own projections make this worse: it forecasts a working capital gap of ₹102.1 cr in FY27 and ₹140.1 cr in FY28 (vs ₹65.1 cr in FY26). This assumes debtor days fall to 100, but also that creditor days collapse from 181 to 30 (S1).

Restatement notes add to the caution. FY26 accounts were audited by AARSH & Associates and then re-audited for the IPO by the peer-review auditor Himanshu Mohta & Associates. The RHP flags as a risk that the restated statements are signed by a CA who is not the statutory auditor (S1). Quarterly stock statements filed with the bank for Q4 FY24 overstated receivables by ₹2.56 cr and inventories by ₹2.11 cr compared with the books (S1).
Verdict on financials: reported profit growth is real on paper, but no cash has come from it yet. Until receivables convert, the FY25–FY26 earnings uplift cannot be treated as proven.

The price band was not in the RHP (dated 19 September 2026) and comes from secondary aggregators. It is recorded here only for completeness, not as a basis for the call.

subsections.title: Objects of the issue in full

blocks.caption: Use of net proceeds (₹ crore, per RHP)

Imported line from ChinTiyan New Energy (Hubei) ₹10.78 cr incl. ₹0.89 cr customs duty, plus ₹2.20 cr utilities, DG set, forklift and BIS/IEC testing. No orders placed

blocks.text: The objects breakdown is from the RHP (S1), and Chittorgarh's summary matches it (S3). IPO Watch prints different figures (debt ₹2.60 cr, working capital ₹24.59 cr), which appear to come from an earlier draft and should be ignored (S4). The capex implementation schedule is: order in October 2026, delivery January 2027, installation February 2027, trial run March 2027, commercial operation April 2027 (S1).

Two-thirds of the named uses (₹29.5 cr of ₹44.6 cr) plug working capital created by slow government collections. The capex (~₹13 cr) builds module capacity in a crowded, commoditised segment. Quotations are budgetary, the proposed supplier is not bound, and the 100 MW line still needs BIS, PID and salt-mist certification after trial runs (S1).

Under SEBI ICDR Regulation 238(a) as stated in the RHP, the minimum promoter contribution of 44,21,940 shares (20% of post-issue capital) is locked in for three years. Of the promoters' remaining holding, 50% is locked for two years and 50% for one year from allotment (S1). Anchor shares are locked 50% for 30 days and 50% for 90 days (S1, S7). According to one aggregator, those unlock on 30 October 2026 and 29 December 2026 (S7).

items: Promoter-contribution shares are all bonus shares from 14 June 2025, which the RHP confirms are eligible under Reg. 237 (S1).
There are only 8 shareholders pre-IPO, so apart from promoters there is no pre-IPO investor overhang (S1).

blocks.text: SME lock-ins are shorter than mainboard. Half of the promoters' excess holding becomes free after one year, and anchor shares free up within 90 days of allotment (S1).

subsections.title: Who runs the company and who owns it

blocks.caption: Promoters and key people (from RHP)
rows: Promoter; not a director; OFS seller

blocks.text: The operating team has relevant but modest credentials. None of the executive promoters has run a listed company or a scaled manufacturing business, and the MD's prior experience is in heating appliances (S1). The most technically credentialed person on the board is an independent director, Dr Oruganti, a former NISE head (S1). The CFO (Sakshi Sharma) has been with the company since 2016. The CS and CFO were formally appointed only in December 2024, ahead of the IPO (S1).

The ownership structure is unusual. The majority owner is a 76-year-old non-director from Karnataka with no other ventures, whose stake came largely through gifts from other individuals (Sahana Lakshmi Mahalinga, Hemalatha). She is also the only seller in the OFS (S1). The RHP does not explain her link to the operating promoters in Haryana. Investors should ask who controls the company economically.

The related-party section is routine (S1). The main item is an unsecured working-capital loan from the MD (₹3.05 cr outstanding at FY26), which supports the company rather than draining it. There are no promoter-linked customers or suppliers, the company has no subsidiaries or group companies, and executive pay is modest compared with profits. Common directorships (Damview Estates, Y P Infra Tech; Ghaf Energy until February 2026) are disclosed, and no transactions with them are recorded (S1).
There is no evidence of value leaking through related parties. The governance concerns are in compliance and ownership, not RPTs.

items: Section 42 contravention: money from two private-placement allotments went into the current account instead of a separate account, and in one case was used before allotment was completed. A compounding/adjudication application was filed on 2 April 2025, the last hearing was on 11 June 2026, and the order is pending (S1).
GST: a show-cause notice (June 2025) alleged ITC 'availed on the strength of fake invoices'. An assessment order for ₹21.30 lakh IGST was passed on 24 December 2025 and is still pending (S1).

Criminal complaint by HVR Solar Pvt Ltd against the company and others (including a senior manager) over ~₹34 lakh of modules and two ₹17.44 lakh cheques that were stopped. It is at the evidence stage, with the next hearing on 23 November 2026 (S1).
Repeated late RoC filings, e.g. AOC-4 filed 11 and 62 days late for FY17 and FY18; late fees were paid (S1).
Stock statements submitted to the bank did not match the restated books, e.g. Q4 FY24 receivables of ₹43.01 cr vs ₹40.45 cr (S1).
A consumer complaint (₹2.7 lakh plus compensation) from a farmer whose subsidised pump was never installed (S1).

blocks.text: No single item is large in money terms: total litigation against the company is ₹59.99 lakh (S1). Together, though, they describe a company with weak internal controls on capital raising, tax documentation and lender reporting. That matters for a business whose working capital depends on bank lines and whose revenue depends on government audits (S1).
Governance quality is below average even for an SME IPO. The GST fake-invoice ITC finding and the Section 42 breach are the two items most likely to recur or escalate.

items: 1. Policy cliff: almost all revenue comes from PM-KUSUM Component-B tenders. The current phase ran until 31 March 2026, and Phase II had not been notified as of mid-September 2026 (S9, S12, S1).
2. Customer concentration: one agency (HAREDA) was 50–88% of revenue across three years, the top 10 customers were 100%, and government was 97% (S1).
3. Cash conversion: debtor days of 269, negative three-year operating cash flow, ~₹60 cr invoiced in Q4 FY26 against projects not yet at payment milestones, and ₹17 cr in retentions (S1).
4. Order book quality: ~₹95 cr of the ₹140 cr backlog is two private module orders with no execution since July 2025. The government pump backlog is small (S1).

5. Expansion execution: the 100 MW line has no orders placed, uses imported machinery exposed to currency moves, needs post-trial certifications, and is expanding capacity when the company's previous module line ran at under 25% utilisation (S1).

6. Technology and regulatory obsolescence: an MNRE efficiency-norm change already made the 40 MW polycrystalline plant obsolete in 2024. A further shift (e.g. to TOPCon or ALMM List-II cell rules) could strand the mono-PERC line (S1).
7. Governance and compliance: the pending Section 42 adjudication, the GST fake-invoice ITC order, a criminal complaint against the company, and lender-reporting mismatches (S1).
8. Supplier credit dependence: creditor days of 181 funded FY26 growth, and the company itself plans to cut this to 30 days, which would need large amounts of new working capital (S1).

blocks.text: Risks 1–3 compound one another. If new tenders slow while old receivables are still being collected, the company would need to raise capital again soon after listing.

Some of the RHP's risk factors are generic and do not change the decision: weather, general competition, and the 'we may not pay dividends' item. The company has never paid a dividend and has no formal dividend policy (S1). Mitigants are real but limited. Maharashtra entry reduced dependence on Haryana from 86% to 53% in one year, net debt is low relative to equity after the issue, and the tender win rate shows the company can compete on price (S1).

items: Contingent liabilities: bank guarantees of ₹29.18 cr (62% of FY26 net worth) would crystallise only if the company fails to perform on its contracts (S1).
Locked-in promoters hold 70.13% after the issue, which aligns them with minority holders at least over the one-to-three-year lock-in window (S1).

blocks.text: These are SME-platform shares: a minimum retail application of ~₹2.47 lakh, market-maker liquidity only, and trading in multiples of the lot size, which makes it hard to sell out of a mistake (S3, S18).
Management has given no revenue or profit guidance, and no investor call or interview could be found. Its forward-looking statements are all in the RHP (S1).

items: Capacity: expand Karnal from 60 MW to 160 MW, with commercial operation targeted for April 2027, move to 20BB/25BB glass-to-glass and TOPCon bifacial modules, and use its own-brand modules in its EPC projects (S1).

Working capital: the WC gap is projected to rise to ₹102.1 cr in FY27 and ₹140.1 cr in FY28. Debtor days are expected to fall to ~100 and inventory days to normalise at ~30 as module manufacturing restarts (S1).
Procurement: creditor days to be cut from 181 to ~30 so the company can buy inputs more cheaply, which it says will support margins (S1).

Diversification: expand into more states and into private EPC via a 40-dealer network. It also cites an NSDC MoU to onboard up to 2,00,000 panchayat-level micro-entrepreneurs and a sanction to train 10,000 people under PMKVY 4.0 (S1).
Orders: Letters of Intent for 50 MW of mono-PERC modules, i.e. the AVI Renewable and Ethos Power orders (S1).

blocks.text: The WC projections imply a much larger business by FY28: current assets of ₹176 cr against ₹140 cr at FY26. But the RHP never states the revenue that would support this, and nothing in it addresses the expiry of PM-KUSUM Phase I (S1, S9).

The plan has two legs. One is to keep winning government pump tenders. The other is to turn a module-manufacturing arm, dormant since August 2024, into a growth engine. The first leg depends on Phase II being notified and funded (S12, S17). The second competes against much larger, integrated players that are adding gigawatt-scale module capacity (Shakti 2.2 GW planned, Oswal 2.1 GW) (S10). A 160 MW line is small by comparison.
The skill-development vertical (₹4.0 cr in FY26, and a ₹3.35 cr NSDC order in the book) is a new, government-funded, low-capital line, but it is too small to change the investment case (S1).

What would change the view: PM-KUSUM 2.0 notified with large state allocations, FY27 receivables collected down towards 100 days with positive operating cash flow, and actual dispatches on the ₹95 cr private module orders.

subsections.title: Day-1 subscription, anchors and grey market

blocks.text: This report was written on 26 September 2026, day 2 of a five-day issue that closes on 29 September. Only day-1 data were available, and they are partial. At 5:39 PM on 25 September the issue was subscribed 0.51x overall: bids for 28,20,000 shares against 55,21,200 on offer (S7). Aggregators differ slightly depending on the time of their snapshot. IPO Guru showed 0.48x at 10:05 PM with 674 applications (S8), and IPO Watch showed 0.36x (S5).

Anchors took 7,52,400 shares for ₹7.75 cr on 24 September 2026. Individual anchor names were not in the sources reviewed. Half the anchor shares are locked for 30 days and half for 90 days (S3, S7). As of 25 September, IPO Watch showed no grey market premium ('not started') (S6). Any GMP is unofficial and is not used in this analysis.
Day-1 SME subscription is usually low and most bids come on the last day, so these numbers say little about final demand. Subscription levels do not change the fundamental 'avoid' call.

method: Primary source: the Red Herring Prospectus dated 19 September 2026, downloaded from the company's website and read directly as page images. Sections read: risk factors, capital structure and lock-in, objects of the issue, business, management, promoters, restated financial statements (balance sheet, P&L, cash flow, notes, related-party note, ratio explanations) and outstanding litigation. The industry-report chapter was not read in detail. All financial figures were converted from ₹ lakh to ₹ crore by the analyst. EBITDA, margins, the three-year cash-flow total, order-book splits and Haryana-award shares are the analyst's own arithmetic on source figures. The September 2025 DRHP on NSE archives was located through search but not opened separately, because the later RHP supersedes it. Issue terms, price band, anchor size and subscription were cross-checked across Chittorgarh, IPO Watch, HDFC Sky and IPO Guru. Day-1 subscription figures differ between aggregators because of snapshot timing, and the 5:39 PM HDFC Sky snapshot is used as the main source. IPO Watch's objects-of-issue figures differ from the RHP and were disregarded. The price band (₹98–103) is not in the RHP and comes from aggregators. Industry context comes from MNRE and HAREDA pages, news reports and an IMARC summary. Scheme-wide installed-pump counts could not be tied to a specific fetched page and were left out. Anchor investor names were not found. No management interview or investor call was found. Material gaps: individual anchor names; independent confirmation of PM-KUSUM Phase II status beyond news reports; the precise split of fresh-issue proceeds between general corporate purposes and issue expenses (shown as [●] in the RHP). Valuation metrics volunteered by sources (P/E, market cap, P/B) were deliberately excluded.
